sourceText: On night 46, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the REPUTATION-COMMONS sector. Goods are free, but reputation determines access to projects and audiences. The memorial bore the name of Cory Doctorow; reputation traditions precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children discovered that technology often solves the problem it can measure and moves the conflict into a variable it never measured. Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world. Vei was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Vei had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Vei, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It 231 was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Marae lives anonymously and discovers that materially one can have everything while socially having almost nothing. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ra — Reputation Economy: reputation distributes access and power; At — Attention Economy: attention becomes the scarce resource. Course references included reputation SF; network fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became 232 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Tern observes that the White Hunger is itself a score that evaluates worlds by their usefulness to Aster. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the ALTERATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 233 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. When the threshold closed, Aster remained silent one second longer than protocol required. The children had already noticed that this was her smallest unit of fear. 234 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
